newsitem.title: USA: US jobless jump possible hint of weaker labor mkt.
newsitem.headline: US jobless jump possible hint of weaker labor mkt.

text.p: A surprising jump in U.S. weekly jobless claims in the latest week hinted that the labor market might be cooling slightly and ought to make the Federal Reserve feel even more comfortable about keeping interest rates on hold, economists said.
The Labor Department reported that new claims for state unemployment insurance rose to 347,000 in the latest week from 339,000 a week earlier.
Economists polled by Reuters had estimated, on average, that claims had fallen to 333,000.

"We are a little surprised that claims did not pull back as we had thought the recent pickup was related to weather disruptions in Texas," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc. "Another couple of weeks of reports like this will tell you that things are easing a little."
"It seems that we're moving back to the range of 325,000 to 350,000 for new claims for unemployment insurance," said Samuel Kahan, president of A.S.K. Financial Research Ltd.
Kahan cautioned against reading too much into the weekly fluctuations in initial jobless claims.

"That said, however, the four-week moving average has been running at between 330,000 and 335,000, possibly indicating that some tightness in the labor market is dissipating -- and that's the way the market is looking at these numbers."
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond, which was down 2/32 before the data came out, erased that narrow loss and climbed into the plus column after the claims data were issued.
At 0920 EDT/1320 GMT, the 30-year Treasury bond was trading at 99-12/32, up 6/32 to yield 6.67 percent.
"It's got to make the Fed feel very comfortable about the way things are shaping up," said Glassman.
"The concern has been that the economy was growing too fast, but now it looks as if things have settled down," said Glassman.

"The drop in consumption that we've seen over the last three months might be starting to filter through to the labor market," said Kahan. "The fear has been that the strong economy has created a tight market and that a tight labor market would cause wages to rise and create inflation down the road. If the labor market loosens, that depletes the fear of rising wages. Consequently there's less fear of inflation and interest rates should go lower," he said.
Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi, said the rise in new jobless claims was "a bit of a mystery.

"It's possible that the increase is due to the slowdown in consumer spending that we've had over the last three months," he said. "But the jury is still out on that. Realistically, we know this is still a very strong economy and I don't think we should be expecting it to fall off a cliff."
Rupkey said seasonal factors affecting jobless claims can be erratic.

"You can see claims build up for several weeks and then they can change direction," he said. "I think the better way to look at these numbers is that this (rise in claims) is an anomaly and that the labor market is still quite strong."
